..
Issued at 225 AM CDT Wed Sep 2 2026

A large heat dome remains stalled over the Lower Mississippi 
River Valley south of a slow-moving upper-level low currently in
central Ontario. Quasi-zonal flow remains in place between both
features and atop a stationary front across the central Great 
Lakes. A short-wavelength upper-level trough embedded in the 
zonal flow is currently supporting several clusters of showers 
and storms along the stationary front stretching from 
northwestern Iowa through central Wisconsin. Meanwhile, south of
the front and indeed across our area, it is a warm and muggy 
night with current air temperatures in the mid to upper 70s (dew
points in the low to mid 70s). 

Based on the continued east-northeasterly trajectory of the 
aforementioned shortwave, current expectations are that all 
clusters of showers and storms along the stationary front will 
remain north of our area through the morning hours. Even if any 
outflow makes it to northern Illinois this morning, it should 
be shallow enough to erode fairly quickly. So barring any 
unexpected southward jogs in the thunderstorm clusters or 
stronger southward outflow pushes, today is setting up to be 
another hot and humid day. Compared to yesterday, mixing 
profiles today look a hair deeper which may modestly offset 
evapotranspirational enhancement to dew points. Regardless, will
continue to lean on NAM/HRDPS guidance which shows dew points 
rebounding to the mid to locally upper 70s today. When paired 
with highs in the lower 90s, heat index values should approach 
105F again. For this reason, did expand the inherited Heat 
Advisory to encompass the entire area. If mixing is more 
effective today, suppose a stray shower or storm may attempt to 
develop this afternoon though coverage should be isolated at 
best. 

Tonight, the stationary front will begin a southward sag toward
the Illinois and Wisconsin state line. Broad and largely 
unfocused low- level flow atop the front may encourage the 
development of a shower or thunderstorm near the frontal 
boundary at any time (not unlike what we saw the past few 
nights), so will carry low-end (20%) PoPs north of I-88 through 
daybreak. Otherwise, tonight is setting up to be a repeat of 
early this morning with seasonably warm overnight lows and 
continued muggy conditions. 

Forecast confidence lowers Thursday and Thursday night. 
Deterministic guidance suggests an upper-level shortwave will 
round the ridge toward the Iowa/Wisconsin/northern Illinois 
vicinity toward daybreak accompanied by an uptick in coverage of
showers and storms. Provided this occurs, at least some 
footprint of cloud cover and cooler temperatures would be 
expected across our area lasting into early afternoon. 
Thereafter, guidance is hinting at another upper-level wave 
approaching the Great Lakes by early afternoon which may lead to
another round of storms in the general region lasting through 
the early morning hours of Friday. If convective coverage is 
minimized in the morning, the afternoon round could end up 
fairly problematic with a reservoir of moisture-laden 
instability and increasing deep- layer shear to support all 
modes of severe thunderstorms (including a threat for flash 
flooding). However if the footprint of morning showers and 
storms is vast, could also envision evolution of thunderstorms 
Thursday afternoon being pretty messy with a lower ceiling for 
intensity. At this point, see too many conditionalities to offer
more than broad-brushed chance (20 to 40%) PoPs. Will also hold
off on issuing any new Heat Advisory for parts of the area 
Thursday in favor of evaluating future model trends in potential
convective coverage. 

Friday into Saturday, ensemble guidance suggests the upper- 
level ridge will retrograde westward placing the Great Lakes 
into the precarious upper-level northwest flow regime. With the 
reservoir of moisture-laden instability remaining in place 
across the Great Lakes region, can easily envision several more 
rounds of (severe) storms in the general region through Saturday
night. At least a brief break in the pattern (both with respect
to humidity levels and temperatures) is anticipated early next 
week. 

Borchardt
